analysis.one_liner: Restores the unlimited federal deduction for state and local taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee for the entire two-year Congress after being referred there on the day it was introduced.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2017 tax law capped how much state and local tax people can deduct on their federal returns at $10,000 a year. This bill would erase that cap, letting taxpayers deduct the full amount again. The biggest winners would be itemizing households with large property and income tax bills — concentrated in New York, New Jersey, California, and other high-tax states, and skewed toward higher incomes. The cost would show up as lost federal revenue, borne by everyone else through higher deficits or other taxes.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that itemize and pay more than $10,000 in state and local taxes — mainly higher-income homeowners in high-tax states like New York, New Jersey, and California. The Tax Policy Center and congressional analyses of the cap have found its benefits fall heavily on upper-income households, and the bill's bipartisan sponsorship was led by New York members of both parties [S1][S3][S4].

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the $10,000-per-year cap on the state and local tax deduction for tax years 2018 through 2025, restoring the fully unlimited deduction that existed before the 2017 tax law [S2][S3].
For affected itemizers, every dollar of state and local tax above the cap would again reduce taxable income, cutting their federal tax bill by their marginal tax rate times the excess [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury. Repealing the cap would reduce federal revenue, a cost shared by all current and future federal taxpayers through larger deficits or the need for other taxes or spending cuts. Non-itemizers and households paying less than $10,000 in state and local taxes — the majority of taxpayers — would get nothing directly from the bill.

drawbacks.text: The benefit would go overwhelmingly to households at the top of the income distribution, since they itemize most often and pay the largest state and local tax bills; families that take the standard deduction would receive no benefit at all [S2][S3].
Because the change would be retroactive to the 2017 tax law's effective date, it would unwind revenue that the cap was designed to raise, adding to federal deficits unless offset elsewhere [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a real tax cut to a specific group — affluent itemizers in high-tax states — but does so by giving up federal revenue that everyone else effectively finances. The strongest case for it is fairness of a sort: these taxpayers pay both high state taxes and full federal taxes, and the cap means they are taxed twice on the same income. The strongest case against it is that a broad, untargeted deduction repeal is an inefficient way to help anyone, and the money flows mostly to those who need it least. The bill contains no offsetting revenue, so the trade is straightforward: concentrated tax relief now, larger deficits later.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Nita Lowey of New York introduced the bill on January 3, 2019, the opening day of the 116th Congress, joined by New York Republican Peter King [S1][S3].
It gathered 16 cosponsors — 12 Democrats and 4 Republicans — a bipartisan but small base of support concentrated among members from high-tax states [S4].
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee on January 3, 2019, and the committee took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The bill never reached the House floor and no Senate companion action appears in its record; it expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal taxpayers as a whole, who avoided a revenue loss that would have flowed mainly to high-income households in high-tax states. High earners lose the chance at the deduction, but the general public was never asked to pay for it because the bill never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but lopsided in origin — a New York Democrat and a New York Republican led it, with 12 Democratic and 4 Republican cosponsors — and no vote was ever taken, so no party-line split can be measured from roll calls.

industries.note: These households would recover deductions worth the most in dollar terms, since the value of a full repeal scales with the size of a taxpayer's tax bill and tax rate. The cost is spread across all federal taxpayers through lost revenue.

industries.industry: State and local governments in high-tax states
industries.note: An unlimited federal deduction softens the perceived cost of state and local taxes for upper-income residents, making it easier for those governments to maintain or raise taxes. The benefit reaches those governments indirectly, through their taxpayers.

industries.industry: Real estate markets in high-tax states
industries.note: Economists linked the 2017 cap to softer home prices and slower sales in expensive markets; a repeal would remove that drag on sellers in New York, New Jersey, and California. Owners in those markets would gain; renters and buyers would see little direct effect.
